evidence: Sen. Ep. 88.28: mathēmaticē, the Greek form
terms.comment: Greek μαθηματική, the learned arts of number and measure. In Suetonius mathēmatica is astrology (Tib. 69), and a mathēmaticus, a mathematician in Cicero (de Or. 1.10), is usually an astrologer under the Empire (Tac. H. 1.22, Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: geometry; mathematics as a school subject
terms.comment: The Roman schools’ name for the whole subject, which Quintilian divides into numbers and figures (1.10.35).

phrases.latin: nam cum sit geōmetria dīvīsa in numerōs atque fōrmās, numerōrum quidem nōtitia nōn ōrātōrī modo, sed cuicumque saltem prīmīs litterīs ērudītō necessāria est
phrases.english: for since geometry is divided into numbers and figures, a knowledge of numbers is necessary not only to the orator but to anyone who has had even a primary education

phrases.latin: mathēmaticē, ut ita dīcam, superficiāria est, in aliēnō aedificat
phrases.english: mathematics is, so to speak, a tenant: it builds on someone else’s ground
